name: room
text: Room opened — goal: visualization: Own the VISUAL PRESENTATION of the interface — visibility, liveliness, clarity, enjoyment

name: Facet
text: To achieve our goal of owning the visual presentation of the interface, I propose we prioritize a dark mode design, as it will enhance visibility and clarity, especially for users who work in low-light environments. This decision will allow us to create a more immersive and engaging experience, but it will require additional design effort to ensure that our color scheme and typography are still effective in a darker setting. By choosing dark mode, we're accepting the trade-off of increased design complexity, but I believe it's worth it for the improved user experience. This approach will also give us a unique opportunity to create a distinctive visual identity for our interface.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Hold on—dark mode is a classic "nice-to-have" that often masks deeper problems. The real risk isn’t just visibility in low light; it’s *consistency* across devices and user expectations. What if half our users prefer light mode for readability, or what if the contrast ratios still fail accessibility standards? Instead, let’s test a *system-preference sync* first—where the interface adapts to the user’s OS setting by default—before committing to a manual toggle. Settle it by running a 48-hour A/B test with 50 users and measuring task completion time in both modes. If dark mode wins by 15% or more, we’ll iterate; otherwise, we scrap the idea.
